title: City Council Approves Pilot Program to Curb Waze Traffic on Side Streets
publisher: NBC Los Angeles (KNBC) / City News Service
authority_names: Los Angeles City Council, Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT)
factual_summary: On April 30, 2019, the Los Angeles City Council voted 12–0 to create a pilot that would seek restrictions on navigation-app routing onto selected streets as a condition of data-sharing agreements. Councilmember Paul Krekorian advocated talks with app developers to address neighborhood traffic and safety concerns. The article notes that the city’s earlier Waze agreement ran from 2015 to 2017. Waze said it was willing to discuss cooperation.

measures.actor: Los Angeles City Council (Councilmember Paul Krekorian) & Mapping Application Developers
measures.mechanism: Contractual conditioning of municipal traffic data-sharing agreements on app developers restricting vehicle routing onto specified residential side streets.
measures.purpose: Curtail side-street traffic flooding and protect residential neighborhood traffic safety.
measures.authority_names: Los Angeles City Council, Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT)
measures.implementation_dates: Approved by City Council on April 30, 2019 (referencing 2015-2017 earlier data agreement)
measures.reported_effects: Anticipated reduction in app-directed cut-through traffic through city-tech dialogue.
measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: None demonstrated; no empirical traffic counts or algorithm-compliance audits reported.

community_feedback.who_expressed: Los Angeles neighborhood residents across residential districts
community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Navigation applications such as Waze causing severe traffic headaches and a flood of cut-through vehicles on tiny side streets not designed for heavy traffic.
community_feedback.which_measure: App-directed cut-through routing and municipal negotiations over data-sharing restrictions.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Council vote approving pilot program conditioning data-sharing agreements
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: With mobile traffic applications such as Waze causing a flood of traffic on tiny side streets, the City Council Tuesday approved a pilot program to restrict the routing of vehicles onto certain streets as a condition of entering into data-sharing agreements with developers of mobile mapping applications.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Councilman Krekorian rationale and unanimous 12-0 vote
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: "There are tremendous advantages to apps like Waze," Councilman Paul Krekorian said last year when discussing his motion that led to Tuesday's 12-0 vote to create the pilot. "They can make driving more efficient, but with every technological advance, any consequences that arise must be taken into account."

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Aiming for municipal-tech dialogue to increase neighborhood safety
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: He added that the city "will have the go-ahead to start a dialogue with these tech companies to see if they will work more closely with us to reduce the impact their apps are having on small residential streets and increase the level of traffic safety in our neighborhoods."

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Prior data agreement history and Waze corporate response
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: Los Angeles had a data-sharing agreement with Waze from 2015 through 2017. "We comply with local laws and regulations where applicable and are always happy to have a dialogue with cities," a Waze spokesperson told NBC4 in a statement.

unresolved_questions: Whether mapping platforms formally signed data-sharing agreements containing restrictive routing clauses.
Legal viability of conditioning public data feeds on proprietary algorithmic routing behavior.
relevance_rationale: Municipal city council legislative action and legal initiatives addressing navigation platform cut-through traffic on neighborhood streets.

title: New Jersey Town Closes Some City Streets to Drivers Who Don’t Live There
actual_jurisdiction: Borough of Leonia, Bergen County, New Jersey
authority_names: Borough of Leonia (Borough Council & Leonia Police Department)
factual_summary: Leonia, New Jersey, began barring out-of-town drivers from 60 streets during morning and evening rush hours on the Monday described in the article, with a threatened $200 fine. Officials blamed navigation-app shortcuts toward the George Washington Bridge for congestion and emergency-access problems. Residents were to display yellow vehicle tags, and Waze said it would mark the streets as restricted. Officials defended the restrictions while critics questioned their legality.

measures.actor: Borough of Leonia Municipal Officials and Leonia Police Department
measures.mechanism: Physical/regulatory closure of 60 streets to out-of-town drivers during morning/evening commute hours, enforced via yellow resident vehicle tags and $200 fines, reflected in Waze as restricted access.
measures.purpose: Prevent hundreds of thousands of navigation-app drivers bypassing I-95/GWB congestion from overwhelming residential streets and blocking emergency responders.
measures.authority_names: Borough of Leonia (Borough Council & Leonia Police Department)
measures.implementation_dates: Effective Monday, January 22, 2018 (rush hours: 6-10 AM and 4-9 PM)
measures.reported_effects: Waze updated maps to reflect 60 streets as restricted access; residents reported relief from gridlock.
measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: None demonstrated; no independent causal before-after traffic counts or regional spillover studies included.

community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Trapped in driveways due to bumper-to-bumper cut-through traffic, with emergency medical and fire vehicles unable to access residential streets.
community_feedback.which_measure: Navigation app shortcuts through borough streets.

community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Illegality and inequity of closing publicly funded streets to non-residents, raising fundamental questions about public right-of-way ownership.
community_feedback.which_measure: Leonia's 60-street resident-only rush hour ban.

community_feedback.who_expressed: Municipal peers (e.g. Takoma Park, MD Public Works)
community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Enforceability dilemmas of 'No through traffic' rules, which require stopping every vehicle unlike simple turn restrictions.
community_feedback.which_measure: Municipal street access restrictions targeting through-traffic.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: 60-street rush-hour ban on non-resident drivers with $200 fine
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: Residents of Leonia, New Jersey, are fed up with traffic apps that treat their small borough as a shortcut to the nearby George Washington Bridge. Starting Monday, officials began banning out-of-town drivers from using 60 streets during morning and evening rush hours, and threatened violators with a $200 fine.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: App-driven traffic volume and severe resident impact quoted by Police Chief Rowe
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: “Without question, the game changer has been the navigation apps,” Tom Rowe, Leonia’s police chief, told the Times. “In the morning, if I sign onto my Waze account, I find there are 250,000 ‘Wazers’ in the area. When the primary roads become congested, it directs vehicles into Leonia and pushes them onto secondary and tertiary roads. We have had days when people can’t get out of their driveways.”

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Vehicle tag mechanism and Waze restricted-access display
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: This week, Leonia residents will begin displaying yellow tags on their cars, signaling to police that they belong on the “shut-down” streets. The road closures will show up on the Waze app as restricted access streets, according to a Waze spokesperson.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Legal pushback and potential court challenges to street closure
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: Borough officials claim the new measure is legal, but it could be tested in court — especially if it sets a precedent for other traffic-app weary towns across the country.

unresolved_questions: Whether the ordinance survived subsequent legal challenge by the New Jersey Attorney General or state courts.
Net diversion volume forced onto neighboring corridors (e.g. Fort Lee, Englewood, I-95 mainlines).
relevance_rationale: Landmark municipal ordinance restricting residential cut-through streets to residents during peak commute hours to counter navigation apps.

title: Delridge Neighborhood Greenway | 26th Ave SW Proposed Diverters: Outreach Summary
authority_names: Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), Seattle City Council
factual_summary: Seattle’s transportation department paused planned traffic diverters at 26th Avenue SW and SW Brandon and SW Genesee streets after residents raised access concerns. Its November 2020 outreach report compares the original diverters, modified diverters and a local-traffic-only Stay Healthy Street. An online survey received 293 responses, with most respondents dissatisfied with each concept; the Stay Healthy Street drew the most support among the alternatives. The department planned to use the feedback in deciding the next safety treatment.

measures.actor: Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) & Seattle City Council
measures.mechanism: Physical traffic diverters (curb and post barriers restricting vehicle turns to right-in/right-out) to separate bike/pedestrian movements and block through-traffic.
measures.purpose: Decrease cut-through traffic along the 26th Ave SW neighborhood greenway and improve bicycle/pedestrian safety.
measures.authority_names: Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), Seattle City Council
measures.implementation_dates: City Council proviso February 21, 2020; flyering July 23, 2020; construction halted July 28, 2020; outreach survey Sept 25 - Oct 15, 2020.
measures.reported_effects: Anticipated reduction in cut-through traffic and safer pedestrian/cyclist conditions.
measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: None demonstrated; project halted prior to construction due to community opposition.

community_feedback.who_expressed: Delridge neighborhood residents (87.37% living near route; 293 survey respondents, 32 meeting participants)
community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Inconvenience from lost turn access; loss of Delridge playfield parking; and concern that restricting 26th Ave SW would simply push cut-through traffic onto 25th Ave SW, a much narrower residential street.
community_feedback.which_measure: Proposed traffic diverters at SW Brandon St and SW Genesee St on 26th Ave SW.

community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Questioned necessity of physical barriers; suggested retiming the traffic light at Brandon/Delridge to reduce cut-through incentive or installing a traffic circle/4-way stop.
community_feedback.which_measure: SDOT traffic diverter designs.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Origin and goal of 26th Ave SW traffic diverters
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: Ultimately, SDOT decided to use diverters at SW Brandon St and SW Genesee St on 26th Ave SW as a way to improve safety. A traffic diverter is made up of a curb and post that is designed to separate vehicle and bicycle traffic. The goal of the diverters along 26th Ave SW was to decrease cut-through traffic along the street and keep people walking, biking, and rolling safely.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Community pushback and decision to pause/halt installation
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: As we started public notification for installation on the diverters, we heard from many community members that they wanted to keep the current access they had at these two intersections, while the diverters restricted some turning movements. In response, we paused installation of the diverters to continue the conversation about how we can work together to make 26th Ave SW safer for people walking and biking.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Outreach timeline and halting notification date
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: 7.28.20 Email Notified neighbors that SDOT would be halting construction of diverters.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Survey results: Resident dissatisfaction and concern about diversion to 25th Ave SW
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: The biggest reasons against options one and two (diverters and modified diverters) was inconvenience to the people that lived there and over 10 people mentioned that reducing traffic on 26th Ave SW will just divert traffic to 25th Ave SW, a narrower street, and not actually fix the traffic problem in the area.

unresolved_questions: Whether SDOT ultimately replaced the diverters with a Stay Healthy Street or traffic circle.
Whether Delridge Way signal retiming was evaluated as an alternative mitigation.
relevance_rationale: Targeted traffic engineering measures (one-way street conversions and physical diverters) installed to block navigation app bypass routes.

title: Waze Connected Citizens Program - United States - Waze Discuss
actual_jurisdiction: Multi-jurisdiction / United States (Inaugural partners: Boston, Los Angeles County, NYPD, Florida DOT, Utah, Kentucky)
authority_names: Waze Mobile Ltd (Google), Boston, Los Angeles County, Miami, New York City / NYPD, Pittsburgh, Florida DOT, Utah DOT, Kentucky Transportation Cabinet
factual_summary: In a December 8, 2014 Waze community post, MGODLEW described the Connected Citizens Program as an exchange of incident and road-closure information between Waze and government partners. The post listed ten initial partners, including Boston, Florida, Utah, Los Angeles County and the New York Police Department, and encouraged members to approach local agencies about joining. The post said sharing data could improve traffic information and incident response.

measures.actor: Waze / Google and Municipal & State Transportation Agencies
measures.mechanism: Bilateral real-time data-sharing agreement: public agencies exchange closure and construction data in return for real-time crowdsourced traffic telemetry at no taxpayer cost.
measures.purpose: Optimize urban traffic flow, speed emergency response to incidents, and route navigation-app users around construction and bottlenecks.
measures.authority_names: Waze Mobile Ltd (Google), Boston, Los Angeles County, Miami, New York City / NYPD, Pittsburgh, Florida DOT, Utah DOT, Kentucky Transportation Cabinet
measures.target_location: Boston, Los Angeles County, Miami, New York City, Pittsburgh; Florida, Utah, Kentucky
measures.implementation_dates: Officially launched October 1, 2014 ('W10' cohort); ongoing municipal onboarding 2014-2015+
measures.reported_effects: Asserted to 'save everyone time and gas money on their daily commute' and build 'more efficient cities'.
measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: None demonstrated; no empirical traffic impact studies or system-level delay evaluations reported.

community_feedback.who_expressed: Volunteer Waze map editors (Champs and State Managers like MGODLEW, dmcrandall, AlanOfTheBerg)
community_feedback.what_concerned_them: How to recruit hesitant municipal DOTs; standardizing partnership outreach templates; coordinating official wiki documentation; ensuring accurate map representation of local road networks.
community_feedback.which_measure: Waze Connected Citizens Program government data partnerships.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Waze Connected Citizens bilateral data exchange program launch
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: The Waze Connected Citizens program brings cities and citizens together to answer the questions “What’s happening, and where?” We exchange publicly available incident and road closure reports, enabling our government partners to respond more immediately to accidents and congestion on their roads. In turn, we aggregate our partners’ data on the Waze platform, resulting in one of the most succinct, thorough overviews of current road conditions today.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Claimed benefits for drivers and municipal traffic planning
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: With the addition of city data, Wazers will be even safer on the roads and more knowledgeable about construction, marathons, floods or anything else that can cause delays. And for our government partners, publicly-available Waze data is a powerful tool to build more efficient cities.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Inaugural government and municipal partners across the US
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: Several major cities & government agencies have already began partnering with Waze including Boston, Miami, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh, New York City & the NYPD. Additionally, the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet along with the Florida Department of Transportation have partnered with Waze as well with no costs to the taxpayers.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Community template for volunteer outreach to local DOTs
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: I’d like to share a generalized template I created for those who wish to reach out to their local Government Agencies & Cities or Department of Transportation. > Dear Mayor / Government Agency Name, > I am reaching out to you to see if [Agency Name] would be interested in considering a partnership with Waze.

quality_flags.signal: Page metadata contained more than one publication date: 2014-12-08, 2015-02-22, 2015-02-23, 2015-03-16, 2015-03-17, 2015-03-24

unresolved_questions: Whether data sharing provided cities any contractual leverage to limit routing through quiet residential neighborhoods.
Whether municipal road closure data accelerated cut-through diversion onto parallel local streets.
relevance_rationale: Bilateral public-private data partnership integrating municipal road closure data with crowdsourced app telemetry to optimize traffic flow.

title: Communication from Public: Council File #11-2130-S4 (Rowena Ave / Angus St Cut-Through Mitigation)
publisher: Los Angeles City Clerk / Silver Lake Neighborhood Council
actual_jurisdiction: City of Los Angeles, California (Silver Lake, Council District 4)
authority_names: Silver Lake Neighborhood Council, Los Angeles City Council, Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT)
factual_summary: The Silver Lake Neighborhood Council voted 18–0 on June 18, 2019 to support retaining Rowena Avenue’s road configuration and adding pedestrian, bicycle and lighting improvements. Its community impact statement also supported a westbound one-way section of Angus Street between Moreno Drive and Kenilworth Avenue, sidewalk feasibility work and further study near Waverly Drive and Glendale Boulevard. The council submitted its statement to the Los Angeles City Clerk on June 24.

measures.actor: Silver Lake Neighborhood Council, Los Angeles City Council (CD4), LADOT
measures.mechanism: Converting Angus Street between Moreno Dr and Kenilworth Ave to a one-way westbound street; installing pedestrian-scale lighting and crosswalks; studying traffic calming at Waverly Dr and Glendale Blvd.
measures.purpose: Mitigate dangerous speeding cut-through bypass traffic displaced from Rowena Avenue onto local residential streets.
measures.authority_names: Silver Lake Neighborhood Council, Los Angeles City Council, Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT)
measures.implementation_dates: Approved 18-0 by SLNC Governing Board on June 18, 2019; submitted to City Clerk on June 24, 2019.
measures.reported_effects: LADOT confirmed reduction in collision frequency on Rowena Avenue, but noted concurrent increase in bypass traffic on local streets.
measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: None demonstrated for proposed one-way conversion; observational collision reduction documented on re-engineered arterial.

community_feedback.who_expressed: Silver Lake Neighborhood Council and Angus Street residents (Katie Singh, Annie Field)
community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Constant fear for children's lives due to speeding bypass cut-through traffic, ignored stop signs, and driver hostility (honking and yelling) toward residents backing out of garages.
community_feedback.which_measure: Council File 11-2130-S4 / Cut-through traffic mitigation on Angus Street.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: SLNC Community Impact Statement documenting bypass traffic on Angus Street
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: Importantly, and separate from the road diet, an increase in bypass traffic on the adjacent local streets was also noted by LADOT. On June 13, 2019, stakeholders in attendance (more than 20) at the Committee meeting described the treacherous conditions on Angus Street, community members expressed their fear and specifically that they constantly fear for their own and their children’s lives due to the bypass traffic that speeds on Angus Street.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Direct resident testimony from Angus Street on ignored stop signs and hostility
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: Our home is at the stop sign at the intersection of Angus and Kenilworth that is often ignored. I cannot tell you how many times I've been yelled at, honked at, and called various names, while simply trying to back out of my garage or walk across the street to my house. We've been here since 2013 and while it wasn't great when we moved it, its horrible now. I have two small children, one of whom walks to school in the neighborhood. He has learned to put up his hand to ask cars to stop so he can cross the street (at a stop sign!!) to go home. It's amazing how many cars ignore him. Please help us make our street safe again!

unresolved_questions: Whether LA City Council approved funding for the Angus Street one-way conversion.
Whether navigation apps adjusted routes following the proposed one-way conversion.
relevance_rationale: Analysis of navigation platform routing patterns, feature updates, and commuter navigation behavior.

title: AB-2015 Transportation: third-party navigation applications: pilot study.
publisher: California Legislative Information / CalMatters Digital Democracy
authority_names: California State Legislature, California Department of Transportation (Caltrans), California State Transportation Agency (CalSTA)
factual_summary: California’s AB 2015 page records the bill as chaptered on September 14, 2026. Its summary requires Caltrans, in consultation with state, regional and local authorities, to conduct a pilot study of third-party navigation apps’ effects on highways and local roads, including congestion displacement, infrastructure, safety and emergency response. A study and policy recommendations are due by January 1, 2029, with repeal scheduled for January 1, 2033.

measures.mechanism: Mandated pilot study and legislative report evaluating third-party navigation apps (Waze, Apple Maps, Google Maps) impacts on state highways and local streets, identifying traffic diversion patterns and safety mitigation measures.
measures.purpose: Evaluate diversion of highway traffic onto local streets and develop policy interventions.
measures.implementation_dates: Enacted September 22, 2026; pilot study report due January 1, 2029
measures.reported_effects: Legislative mandate established; study underway.
measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: None yet; empirical evaluation scheduled for 2029 report.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Legislative mandate for Caltrans navigation app pilot study
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: This bill would require the department, in consultation with the Transportation Agency and relevant regional and local authorities, to conduct a pilot study in a region or area of the state, as determined by the department, on the impact of third-party navigation applications on the state highway system and local street and road networks.

unresolved_questions: Which specific California region will Caltrans select for the pilot study?
What data-sharing requirements will be imposed on private navigation platforms?
relevance_rationale: Statutory and legislative mandate requiring navigation platforms to respect municipal street restrictions and commercial bridge heights.

title: Lawmaker warns of proposal that could alter California drivers' commutes: 'Adds 30 minutes'
authority_names: California State Legislature, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, Assemblymember Carl DeMaio
factual_summary: California Assemblymember Carl DeMaio criticized AB 2015 in a social-media video, warning that studying navigation apps could eventually lead to government-directed routes and longer commutes. Nina Joudeh’s June 16, 2026 report explains that the proposal then imposed no immediate restrictions on navigation platforms. It called for Caltrans and other authorities to study app effects and report recommendations by January 1, 2028. DeMaio warned that government-directed routes could add 30 minutes to commutes.

measures.mechanism: State legislation studying and potentially regulating navigation app routing algorithms to prevent commuter cut-through traffic.
measures.purpose: Mitigate neighborhood traffic infiltration from freeway spillover.
measures.reported_effects: Critics claim 30-minute commute increases if detours are restricted.

community_feedback.who_expressed: Assemblymember Carl DeMaio and commuter advocates
community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Concerns that state restrictions on navigation apps like Google Maps and Apple Maps will artificially worsen highway gridlock and lengthen commutes by 30 minutes.
community_feedback.which_measure: California Assembly Bill 2015

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Commuter opposition and warning regarding navigation app regulation
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: sounding the alarm over a Democratic-backed proposal to study how navigation apps like Apple Maps and [Google Maps affect state traffic patterns](https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/google-maps-slammed-hiding-brutal-174711234.html), a move he says could potentially add "[30 minutes to your commute](https://nypost.com/2026/03/19/opinion/miserable-driving-in-la-now-just-wait/)."

unresolved_questions: Whether the final statute incorporated commuter protection safeguards against artificial travel delays.
relevance_rationale: Statutory and legislative mandate requiring navigation platforms to respect municipal street restrictions and commercial bridge heights.

title: Motion 14-1741-S1 (Data-Sharing Partnership with Waze to Protect Residential Streets)
authority_names: Los Angeles City Council, Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT)
factual_summary: A Los Angeles transportation motion sought a report from the Department of Transportation on the city’s announced data-sharing partnership with Waze. It asked whether expanding that partnership could reduce cut-through vehicle traffic diverted onto residential streets. The motion contrasted high-capacity roads with smaller streets lacking comparable pedestrian protections and suggested that the city might use its partnership to influence routing.

measures.mechanism: Directing LADOT to structure data-sharing agreements with Waze and mapping apps to protect residential streets from navigation detour routing.
measures.purpose: Prevent navigation apps from funneling arterial traffic onto narrow hillside and residential streets.
measures.reported_effects: Initiated municipal negotiations with Waze.

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Mayor and LADOT partnership announcement with Waze
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: During the State of the City address and in subsequent days, the Mayor announced a partnership between the Department of Transportation and Waze, a popular mapping app, which would share up-to-the-minute city traffic data with Waze.

unresolved_questions: What formal concessions did LADOT extract from Waze following this motion?
relevance_rationale: Bilateral public-private data partnership integrating municipal road closure data with crowdsourced app telemetry to optimize traffic flow.

title: L.A. May Crack Down on Waze and Google Maps
authority_names: Los Angeles City Council, Councilmember Paul Krekorian, LADOT
factual_summary: Los Angeles’s City Council directed its transportation department to pursue a pilot involving data sharing with navigation-app makers and restrictions on routing along selected streets. Brittany Martin’s May 7, 2019 article describes residents’ complaints about cut-through traffic, emergency access and neighborhood disruption. It also raises unresolved questions about which streets would absorb displaced traffic and whether app makers would cooperate.

measures.actor: Los Angeles City Council, City Attorney, LADOT
measures.mechanism: Pilot program establishing conditional data-sharing agreements requiring mapping apps to exclude designated residential streets from commuter routing.
measures.purpose: Stop commercial navigation apps from overwhelming residential hillside streets.
measures.reported_effects: Council voted 12-0 to advance conditional data sharing.

community_feedback.who_expressed: Councilmember Paul Krekorian and hillside neighborhood residents
community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Dangerous gridlock, emergency vehicle obstruction, and loss of safety on narrow residential streets caused by app detour suggestions.
community_feedback.which_measure: Los Angeles conditional data-sharing pilot program

supporting_passages.claim_topic: LA City Council pilot program targeting navigation app algorithms
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: A pilot program launched by L.A.’s City Council could bring big changes to the workings of directions apps like Waze and Google Maps.

unresolved_questions: Whether tech companies agreed to the conditional data terms or refused access.

title: Waze Hijacked L.A. in the Name of Convenience. Can Anyone Put the Genie Back in the Bottle?
authority_names: Los Angeles City Council, LADOT, Waze / Google
factual_summary: Jonathan Littman’s August 2019 feature describes Los Angeles residents’ complaints that navigation apps increased traffic on narrow residential streets. It examines volunteer map editing, residents’ attempts to change routes and researchers’ concerns about individually optimized routing. The city had let its earlier Waze agreement expire and was pursuing a new pilot under Councilmember Paul Krekorian, with LADOT seeking cooperation from app companies. Waze said it was committed to working with cities.

measures.purpose: Mitigate commuter cut-through speeding prompted by routing algorithms.

measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: Observational only; traffic displaced to adjacent blocks.

measures.mechanism: Guerrilla reporting of fake accidents, blocked roads, and hazards into Waze app.
measures.purpose: Trick Waze algorithms into diverting commuters away from residential neighborhoods.
measures.reported_effects: Short-term routing shifts; Waze algorithm flagged and suppressed fraudulent user accounts.

title: 'Absolute chaos': Navigation apps blamed for traffic nightmare on one of L.A.'s steepest streets
actual_jurisdiction: City of Los Angeles, California (Echo Park)
authority_names: Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT), KTLA
factual_summary: Residents of Baxter Street in Los Angeles’s Echo Park neighborhood told KTLA that navigation-app shortcuts were bringing unfamiliar drivers onto its steep roadway, where they reported crashes and spinouts. Residents supplied photographs and video of incidents and said they had asked Waze to stop treating the street as a shortcut. A meeting with Councilmember Mitch O’Farrell and transportation officials was planned, with a one-way conversion among the options discussed.

measures.mechanism: Converting Baxter Street to a one-way westbound street and installing high-visibility warning signage and grooved pavement.
measures.purpose: Prevent dangerous downhill spinouts and rollovers caused by navigation apps routing drivers down extreme 32% grades.
measures.reported_effects: Reduced head-on collisions, but navigation apps continued sending downhill traffic resulting in rain spinouts.
measures.demonstrated_causal_effects: One-way flow eliminated opposing-traffic collisions, but downhill accidents persist.

community_feedback.what_concerned_them: Repeated car spinouts into front yards, flipped vehicles, property damage, and intense fear during rainstorms due to commuter app navigation.
community_feedback.which_measure: Baxter Street one-way conversion and navigation app routing

supporting_passages.claim_topic: Baxter Street cut-through traffic attributed to navigation apps
supporting_passages.verbatim_text: The road in question is Baxter Street in Echo Park.

unresolved_questions: Why navigation algorithms fail to account for road slope/grade when calculating optimal detours.
relevance_rationale: Severe physical traffic hazards and vehicle rollovers on extreme-gradient residential streets caused by routing algorithm shortcuts.

title: Walsh announces partnership with traffic app, Waze
authority_names: City of Boston, Mayor Martin J. Walsh, Boston Transportation Department
factual_summary: Boston Mayor Martin Walsh announced a data-sharing partnership with Waze under its Connected Citizens program. City officials said they would send expected road closures to app users and use incoming traffic reports in the Traffic Management Center, where engineers could adjust signals at 550 intersections. The February 19, 2015 report quotes supporters expecting better traffic information and incident responses, while Tufts professor Julian Agyeman argued for reducing traffic rather than only managing it.

measures.actor: City of Boston (Mayor Martin J. Walsh), Waze
measures.mechanism: Two-way data exchange sharing municipal road closures with Waze in exchange for crowdsourced traffic speed and incident data.
measures.purpose: Improve municipal traffic operations, reduce congestion, and optimize traffic signal timing.

title: University of Michigan: Truck Noise in Southwest Detroit Adds to Public Health Concerns
factual_summary: University of Michigan researchers and Southwest Detroit residents measured noise at 21 homes to study truck-traffic impacts. They combined sound monitoring, vehicle counts, photographs and Google Maps information and reported higher noise near truck routes, including levels exceeding cited guidelines. Community partners hoped the findings would inform truck-route changes as the Gordie Howe International Bridge was built, while residents described sleep disruption and difficulty using outdoor space.
